title: Basic Tailoring & Garment Repair
subtitle: Sew strong hand and machine stitches, repair and alter everyday clothes to a professional standard, and price your work to earn from home.
description: A practical beginner course in hand sewing, machine use and the repairs customers ask for most: buttons, hems, zips, split seams, tears and side-seam alterations. Thread, adjust and maintain a manual or electric sewing machine
Hem trousers and skirts, sew buttons with a thread shank, replace zips and mend seams and tears

Run each order with a job card, a quality checklist and a costed price

modules.title: Fabrics, Hand Stitches and a Safe, Measured Workspace
modules.overview: Before you touch a machine you need to know your materials, sew strong stitches by hand and measure accurately in centimetres. This module covers the kinds of jobs a home tailor does, how woven and knit fabrics behave, the six hand stitches every repair uses, and how to set up a safe, well-lit work corner.

lessons.title: Repair, alteration and making: the jobs and the fabrics
objectives: Name the three kinds of tailoring work: repair, alteration and simple making
Tell woven fabric from knit fabric and explain why it matters
Find the straight grain, cross grain and bias on a piece of cloth
Choose a sensible first service to offer from home

blocks.text: Almost every household has a pile of clothes waiting for small fixes: a school shirt with a missing button, trousers that are too long, a dress with a split side seam, a bag with a broken zip. A home tailor earns money from three kinds of work. **Repair** brings a damaged garment back to use. **Alteration** changes the fit or length of a garment that is already made. **Making** means cutting and sewing a new item from fabric.

blocks.name: spool-of-thread
blocks.caption: Thread, needle and a little skill turn a pile of damaged clothes into paid work.

blocks.text: Three kinds of work, three levels of skill

head: Type of work
Common jobs
Skill needed
Good first step?
rows: Replace buttons, mend split seams, patch tears, replace zips, darn small holes
Shorten trousers and sleeves, take in or let out side seams, adjust waistbands
Yes, after a few weeks of repairs
Pillowcases, aprons, simple skirts, tote bags, then fitted garments
Simple items only at this level

blocks.text: Repairs need the least equipment and build the habits that alterations and making depend on: straight stitching, neat finishing and careful pressing. This course moves in that order. By the end you will repair, alter and make one simple item to a standard you can charge for.
Woven and knit: the first thing to check

**Woven fabric** is made from threads crossing at right angles, like a mat. Ankara (cotton wax print), shirting, denim, guinea brocade, linen and most uniforms are woven. Woven fabric does not stretch much along its threads, and its cut edges fray. **Knit fabric** is made from loops, like a sweater. T-shirts, jersey gowns, leggings and polo shirts are knits. Knits stretch, and their cut edges usually curl rather than fray.

This matters for every job. Knits need a stitch that can stretch with them, such as a narrow zigzag, and a ballpoint needle that slides between the loops instead of cutting them. Wovens need their raw edges finished so they do not fray in the wash. To test, pull the fabric gently: if it stretches easily and springs back, it is a knit.

Before you accept any garment, look at its care label if it has one. It tells you the fibre (cotton, polyester, viscose, a blend) and how hot it can be ironed. Cotton and linen take a hot iron; polyester and viscose need a cooler setting or they shine and melt. Lace and fabrics with sequins or stones should be pressed from the wrong side through a cloth.
Grain: why fabric hangs straight or twists

items: **Selvedge**: the firm, finished edge on each side of the fabric as it comes off the roll. It does not fray.
**Straight grain (lengthwise grain)**: runs parallel to the selvedge. It is the strongest direction with the least stretch. Most garment pieces are cut with their length on the straight grain.
**Cross grain**: runs from selvedge to selvedge, at right angles to the straight grain. It has a little more give.
**Bias**: any diagonal line; the true bias is at 45 degrees. Woven fabric stretches most on the bias, which is why bias strips curve neatly around necklines.

blocks.text: When you cut a patch or a new piece off grain, it twists after washing and the garment hangs badly. When you repair, try to match the grain of the patch to the grain of the garment.

blocks.title: Woven versus knit fabric
items: Woven
Knit
blocks.caption: Check the fabric type before choosing needle, stitch and finish.

blocks.text: Choosing your first service

A good first service is one you can do well with the tools you have, that people need often, and that you can finish quickly. Button replacement, hemming trousers and mending split seams fit all three. Zips and side-seam alterations come next, once your machine stitching is steady.

blocks.title: Worked example: picking a starting menu
blocks.context: For example, Amaka lives in Onitsha, has a needle set, thread, scissors and a tape measure, and has been offered the use of her aunt's manual sewing machine two afternoons a week.
steps: She lists jobs she sees around her: missing buttons on school shirts, long trousers, split seams on ankara gowns, broken zips on skirts.
She marks which jobs need only hand tools: buttons, small seam repairs and hand hems.
She marks jobs that need the machine: long seams, zips and side-seam alterations.
She starts with buttons and hand hems every day, and saves machine jobs for her two afternoons.
blocks.result: Amaka offers three services from week one (buttons, hand hems, small seam repairs) and adds machine work as her practice grows. Her menu fits her tools and her time.

blocks.title: Keep a sample bag
blocks.text: Ask your local tailor or fabric seller for small offcuts of ankara, shirting, denim, lace and jersey. Label each one woven or knit. You will practise every stitch in this course on scraps before touching a customer's garment.

takeaways: Tailoring work falls into repair, alteration and making; start with repair
Woven fabric frays and barely stretches; knit fabric stretches and curls
Straight grain runs parallel to the selvedge; bias is the diagonal
Choose first services that suit your tools, time and local demand

activity.title: Sort and label your fabric samples
steps: Collect at least six fabric scraps from home, a tailor or a fabric seller.
Do the stretch test on each and label it woven or knit.
On each woven scrap, find the selvedge (if present) and draw an arrow along the straight grain with chalk or pencil.
Pull each woven scrap on the bias and note how much more it stretches.
Write down three repair jobs you have seen in your household or street this month.
activity.evidence: A photo of your labelled scraps with grain arrows, and your list of three local repair jobs.

lessons.title: Six hand stitches every tailor must know
objectives: Thread a needle and tie a secure starting knot
Sew running stitch, backstitch, slip stitch, blind hem stitch, whipstitch and overcast stitch
Choose the right hand stitch for a repair
Finish a line of stitching so it does not unravel

blocks.text: A sewing machine is fast, but many repairs are done by hand: hems on fine fabric, small seam splits, linings, buttons and anywhere the machine cannot reach. Six hand stitches cover nearly every repair you will meet. Learn them on scrap fabric until your stitches are even in size and spacing.

blocks.name: sewing-needle
blocks.caption: Six simple hand stitches handle most everyday repairs.

blocks.text: Getting ready: needle, thread and knot

items: Cut a piece of thread about 45 to 50 cm long, roughly the length from your fingertips to your elbow and back. Longer thread tangles and wears thin as it passes through the fabric.
Cut the end at a slant with sharp scissors so it passes through the needle eye easily.
Thread the needle. For most repairs use a single thread; for buttons, use a double thread (pull the ends together) for extra strength.
Tie a knot at the end: wrap the thread twice around your index finger, roll it off with your thumb, and pull the loop tight.
Start from the wrong side (inside) of the fabric so the knot is hidden.

blocks.title: Match the needle to the fabric
blocks.text: Use a fine, sharp needle for shirting and lace, a medium needle for ankara and cotton, and a thicker needle for denim. Choose thread a shade darker than the fabric; it blends in better than a lighter one.
The six stitches

head: Stitch
How you make it
Use it for
rows: Push the needle in and out along a straight line, making stitches and gaps of equal length (about 3 to 5 mm).
Gathering, temporary basting (tacking) before machine sewing, quick light seams
Make one stitch forward, then bring the needle up one stitch length ahead and go back down at the end of the last stitch, so the stitches touch.
The strongest hand seam; mending split seams, crotch and underarm repairs
Take a small stitch inside the fold on one side, then a small stitch inside the fold directly opposite, like rungs of a ladder. Pull gently and the opening closes invisibly.
Closing a gap in a seam from the outside, closing linings, stuffed items
Take a tiny stitch, just one or two threads, from the garment, then a slightly longer stitch inside the folded hem edge. Repeat about every 1 cm.
Hems on trousers, skirts and dresses where stitches must not show on the outside
Pass the needle over the edge of the fabric and back through from the same side, making slanted stitches.
Joining two finished edges, attaching patches, felt
Like whipstitch but worked over a single raw edge, with stitches about 5 mm apart and 5 mm deep.
Stopping a cut edge from fraying when you have no overlocker or zigzag

blocks.text: Finishing so the stitching holds

A line of stitches is only as strong as its ending. On the wrong side, take a tiny stitch through the last stitch but do not pull it tight. Pass the needle through the loop that forms, then pull firmly. Repeat once more, then trim the thread leaving about 5 mm. This is often called a **knot finish** or **locking stitch**. Never end by simply cutting the thread; the stitches will pull out with the first wash.

blocks.title: Choosing a hand stitch
items: Must it be strong?
Yes: backstitch
Must it be invisible?
Yes: slip or blind hem
Raw edge fraying? Overcast
blocks.caption: Ask what the repair needs most, strength, invisibility or edge control, and pick the stitch that gives it.

blocks.title: Worked example: mending a split underarm seam
blocks.context: For example, Halima's neighbour brings a cotton blouse with a 6 cm split in the underarm seam. The fabric itself is not torn; only the stitching has broken.
steps: Halima turns the blouse inside out and pulls out the loose broken threads so they do not get caught.
She pins the two seam edges together along the original stitching line, which she can still see as small holes.
She starts with a knot about 1 cm before the split, in the old stitching that is still good, so the repair overlaps.
She sews backstitch with stitches about 2 to 3 mm long along the old line, ending 1 cm past the split.
She finishes with two locking stitches and trims the thread, then presses the seam.
blocks.result: The repair overlaps sound stitching by 1 cm at each end, so the seam will not split again at the same point. The job takes about 15 minutes.

blocks.text: Speed comes later. At first, aim for stitches of the same length with the same gaps. A useful habit is to count: for a backstitch seam, about three to five stitches per centimetre on light fabric, fewer on thick denim. Even, small stitches look professional and hold far better than long, uneven ones.

blocks.title: Do not sew too tight
blocks.text: Pulling each stitch hard makes the fabric pucker (wrinkle). Pull until the thread lies flat on the fabric and stop there. Check by laying the work flat: it should not ripple.

takeaways: Use a single thread of 45 to 50 cm for most repairs and a double thread for buttons
Backstitch is the strongest hand seam; slip and blind hem stitches are invisible
Overcast a raw edge when you cannot zigzag or overlock it
Overlap repairs into sound stitching and always finish with locking stitches

activity.title: Make a stitch sampler
steps: Cut a woven scrap about 20 cm by 25 cm and draw six straight lines 3 cm apart with chalk.
Sew one line of each stitch: running, backstitch, slip stitch (on a folded edge), blind hem, whipstitch, overcast.
Label each line with a small paper tag or with the stitch name written in pencil beside it.
Check each line: are the stitches even in length and does the fabric lie flat?
Redo the weakest line until it is even.
activity.evidence: A photo of your finished sampler, front and back, with each stitch labelled.

lessons.title: Measuring in centimetres and setting up a safe work corner
objectives: Take bust, waist, hip, inseam and length measurements correctly in cm
Explain seam allowance and hem allowance
Set up a work corner with the right tools, light and safety habits
Store needles, pins and scissors safely around children

blocks.text: Good tailoring depends on accurate numbers. A mistake of 2 cm at the waist is the difference between a comfortable fit and a garment that will not close. In this lesson you learn to measure a person and a garment in centimetres, and to set up a work corner that keeps you, your family and your customers' clothes safe.

blocks.name: straight-ruler
blocks.caption: Accurate centimetre measurements are the foundation of every alteration.

blocks.text: Your basic tool kit

items: **Tape measure** (150 cm, with cm on at least one side). Replace it if it stretches or the numbers wear off.
**Fabric scissors** used only for fabric; paper dulls them. A small pair of thread snips is handy too.
**Seam ripper** for unpicking stitches without cutting the fabric.
**Pins and a pincushion**, **hand needles** in several sizes and a **thimble** to push the needle through thick cloth.
**Tailor's chalk** or a washable fabric marker, and a ruler (30 cm or a longer metre rule).
**Iron and ironing surface.** Pressing is part of sewing, not an extra.

blocks.text: Taking body measurements

Measure over light clothing, with the tape snug but not tight: you should be able to slide one finger under it. Keep the tape level all the way round. Write every number down at once, in cm, with the customer's name and the date.

head: Measurement
Where to place the tape
rows: Around the fullest part of the chest, under the arms, level at the back
Around the natural waist, the narrowest part of the body, usually just above the navel
Around the fullest part of the hips and bottom, feet together
From the crotch along the inside leg to where the trouser should end, or measure an existing trouser that fits
For a dress or top, from the shoulder at the base of the neck down to the desired hem
From the shoulder point, over a slightly bent elbow, to the wrist bone

blocks.text: Allowances: the extra fabric beyond the stitching line

**Seam allowance** is the distance between the cut edge and the stitching line. Many commercial patterns use 1.5 cm; some use 1 cm. When you take in or let out a garment, the seam allowance is the fabric you have to work with. **Hem allowance** is the fabric folded up at the bottom of a garment. For trousers, about 4 cm is common; for a straight skirt, 4 to 5 cm; for a full or curved skirt, a narrow hem of about 1 to 2 cm sits better.

blocks.title: Worked example: measuring for a trouser hem
blocks.context: For example, Bisi brings her son's school trousers to Fatima, a home tailor. They are 6 cm too long. The current hem is 3 cm deep.
steps: Fatima has the boy wear the trousers with his school shoes and folds the hem up until it just touches the top of the shoe at the front.
She pins it and measures from the old hem edge to the new fold: 6 cm.
She decides on a finished hem allowance of 4 cm.
New cutting line = new fold line + 4 cm of hem allowance. She marks the fold line with chalk, then a second line 4 cm below it.
Old fabric below the new fold is 6 cm + 3 cm old hem = 9 cm. She keeps 4 cm and trims off 5 cm.
blocks.result: Fatima knows exactly where to fold and where to cut before she touches the scissors, so there is no risk of cutting too short.

blocks.title: Measure twice, cut once
blocks.text: Fabric cut too short cannot be put back. Pin, check on the person or against a garment that fits, and measure both legs or both sides before cutting.
A safe, well-lit work corner

blocks.title: Work corner safety check
items: Good light on work
Needles in a closed box
Scissors out of reach
Iron unplugged after use
No trailing cables
Chair supports your back
blocks.caption: Run this check every time you set up to sew.

blocks.text: Good light reduces mistakes and eye strain; sit near a window in the day and use a bright bulb at night. Keep pins and needles in a closed tin, never in your mouth. Pick up dropped pins with a magnet. Keep scissors closed and out of children's reach. An iron is hot enough to burn skin and fabric: stand it upright on its heel, keep the cable away from the edge where a child could pull it, and switch it off at the wall when you finish. When the grid is off and you use a generator, never run it indoors or near windows, because its fumes contain carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas you cannot smell.

blocks.title: Electricity and generators
blocks.text: Never touch an electric machine or iron with wet hands, and unplug them before cleaning. Run any generator outside, away from doors and windows, to avoid carbon monoxide poisoning.

takeaways: Measure snug but not tight, keep the tape level, and write numbers in cm at once
Seam allowance is often 1 to 1.5 cm; trouser hems are usually about 4 cm
Mark the fold line and the cutting line before you cut
Keep needles boxed, scissors out of reach, and irons and generators handled safely

activity.title: Measure and set up
steps: Take bust, waist, hip, sleeve and garment length measurements of one family member and write them in a notebook with name and date.
Measure one pair of trousers that fits well: waist, inseam and hem depth.
Set up your work corner and run the six-point safety checklist.
Put all pins and needles into a closed container.
activity.evidence: A photo of your measurement page and a photo of your work corner showing tools stored safely.

quiz.q: A customer brings a stretchy polo shirt with a split seam. Which choice is best?
options: Straight stitch with a sharp needle
Narrow zigzag with a ballpoint needle
quiz.explain: Polo shirts are knit fabric. A narrow zigzag stretches with the fabric and a ballpoint needle slides between the loops instead of cutting them.

quiz.q: Which hand stitch gives the strongest seam repair?
quiz.explain: In backstitch each stitch touches the one before, giving a continuous line close to machine strength.

quiz.q: Trousers are 6 cm too long and have a 3 cm hem. Keeping a 4 cm hem, how much should be trimmed off?
quiz.explain: Below the new fold there is 6 cm plus the 3 cm old hem, 9 cm in total. Keep 4 cm for the new hem and trim 5 cm.

quiz.q: Where does the straight grain run on woven fabric?
quiz.explain: The straight (lengthwise) grain runs parallel to the selvedge and is the strongest, least stretchy direction.

quiz.q: Halima wants to close a gap in a lining from the outside so no stitches show. Which stitch should she use?
quiz.explain: Slip stitch takes small stitches inside each fold, so when pulled the gap closes invisibly.

quiz.q: What is the safest way to run a generator for your sewing work?
options: Inside the room with the door open
In the kitchen near a window
Outside, away from doors and windows
quiz.explain: Generator fumes contain carbon monoxide, which is poisonous and has no smell. Run it outside, away from openings.

modules.title: The Sewing Machine, Hems, Buttons and Zips
modules.overview: Now you move to the jobs customers ask for most. You will thread and look after a sewing machine, hem trousers and skirts, sew buttons that stay on, replace a zip and mend seams and tears. Each lesson ends with a repair you can photograph for your portfolio.

lessons.title: Threading, tension and caring for your sewing machine
objectives: Name the main parts of a domestic sewing machine
Thread the upper thread and bobbin in the correct order
Read a stitch and correct common tension problems
Clean, oil and change the needle on a regular schedule

blocks.text: In Nigeria you will meet three kinds of machines. **Manual machines** are turned by a hand wheel or a foot **treadle** and need no electricity; the Butterfly brand is a common example in local markets. **Electric domestic machines** from brands such as Singer, Janome and Brother run on a foot pedal and often have zigzag and other stitches. **Industrial straight-stitch machines** are fast, heavy machines used in busy tailoring shops. The threading principles are the same on all of them.

blocks.name: working-at-home
blocks.alt: A woman working at a desk at home
blocks.caption: A sewing machine set up in a quiet corner at home can earn steady income.

blocks.text: Parts you need to know

head: Part
What it does
rows: Holds the reel of thread on top of the machine
Squeeze the upper thread to control how tightly it is pulled into the stitch
Moves up and down, pulling thread through the machine for each stitch
Carry the upper thread down through the fabric
Hold the fabric flat against the feed dogs; raising the lever also opens the tension discs
Small metal teeth under the foot that move the fabric along
Hold the lower thread; the upper and lower threads lock together in the fabric
Turns the needle up and down by hand; always turn it towards you

blocks.text: Threading the upper thread

items: Raise the presser foot. This opens the tension discs so the thread can sit between them. If the foot is down, the thread misses the discs and you get a tangle of loops underneath.
Turn the hand wheel towards you until the needle and the take-up lever are at their highest point.
Place the reel on the spool pin and lead the thread through the top thread guide.
Bring the thread down the channel through the tension area, around the U-turn, and up to the take-up lever. Hook it through the lever's eye or slot.
Bring it down through the guides just above the needle.
Thread the needle. On most modern domestic machines this is front to back; some older machines thread from the side. Check your manual.
Pull about 10 to 15 cm of thread through and lay it under the presser foot.

blocks.text: Winding and inserting the bobbin

Wind thread onto an empty bobbin using the bobbin winder on top of the machine, so the thread goes on evenly and firmly. Insert it as your machine requires: a **drop-in bobbin** sits flat under a clear cover beside the needle plate; a **front-loading bobbin** goes into a separate metal bobbin case behind a small door. Hold the upper thread lightly, turn the hand wheel towards you one full turn, and the needle will bring up a loop of bobbin thread. Pull both threads to the back under the foot.
Reading the stitch and fixing tension

In a balanced stitch, the upper and bobbin threads lock between the two fabric layers, and the stitch looks the same on both sides. Set stitch length to about 2.5 mm for normal seams. At the start and end of every seam, sew three or four stitches in reverse to lock it.

blocks.title: Diagnosing a bad stitch
items: Loops underneath: rethread top
Bobbin thread on top: lower top tension
Skipped stitches: change needle
Thread breaks: check reel, needle
blocks.caption: Most stitch problems come from threading or the needle, not the tension dial.

blocks.title: Worked example: the loops underneath
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi sews a test seam on a scrap of ankara and finds a nest of loose loops on the underside.
steps: She knows loops underneath usually mean a problem with the upper thread, not the bobbin.
She cuts the threads, removes the fabric and raises the presser foot.
She rethreads the top from the beginning, making sure the thread passes through the take-up lever.
She sews another test seam at stitch length 2.5 mm.
blocks.result: The stitch is now balanced on both sides. She did not touch the tension dial, which was never the problem.

blocks.text: Care and maintenance

items: **Unplug** an electric machine before cleaning or changing the needle.
**Clean** lint from the feed dogs and bobbin area with a small brush after every few hours of sewing. Lint build-up causes skipped stitches and noise.

**Oil** only where your manual shows, with sewing machine oil, never cooking oil. Treadle machines have several oil holes. After oiling, sew on a scrap to absorb any extra oil before touching a customer's garment.

**Change the needle** at the start of each big project, after about 8 hours of sewing, or at once if it is bent, blunt or skipping. On most domestic machines the flat side of the needle shank faces the back.
**Cover** the machine when not in use to keep out dust.

blocks.title: Match needle size to fabric
blocks.text: Needles are sized with two numbers, such as 80/12. Use 70/10 for fine shirting and lace, 80/12 for ankara and cotton, 90/14 for heavier cotton, and 100/16 for denim. Use ballpoint needles for knits.

takeaways: Thread with the presser foot up and the needle at its highest point
Loops underneath usually mean the upper thread is wrongly threaded
Sew at about 2.5 mm and lock each seam with a few reverse stitches
Clean lint often, oil only where the manual says, and change needles regularly

activity.title: Thread, test and clean
steps: Wind a bobbin and thread your machine from scratch, following the steps above.
Sew three test lines on a doubled scrap of cotton at 2.5 mm, locking each end.
Photograph both sides of the stitching and check they look the same.
Unplug the machine, remove the needle plate if possible, and brush out the lint.
Write the date and needle size in a small maintenance log.
activity.evidence: Photos of your test stitching (both sides) and your first maintenance log entry.

lessons.title: Hemming trousers and skirts, and sewing on buttons that stay on
objectives: Mark, cut, press and sew a trouser hem to the correct length
Choose between a hand blind hem and a machine hem
Sew a flat button with a thread shank
Cost a hemming job in naira

blocks.text: Shortening trousers and replacing buttons are the two jobs a home tailor gets most often. Both look simple, and both separate careful tailors from careless ones. A hem must be the same length on both legs and must not show on the outside. A button must sit loosely enough to fasten easily and be stitched firmly enough to last.

blocks.name: jeans
blocks.caption: Trousers and jeans that are too long are the most common alteration job.

blocks.text: Hemming trousers: the method

items: Ask the customer to wear the trousers with the shoes they will wear with them. Fold the hem up to the length they want, usually just touching the top of the shoe at the front, and pin.
Measure from the floor or from the old hem to the pinned fold on one leg. Check the other leg on the person too. Never assume both legs are the same length.
Unpick the old hem with a seam ripper and press it flat.
Mark the new fold line with chalk. Measure the hem allowance below it (about 4 cm for trousers) and mark the cutting line. Cut along it.
Finish the raw edge: zigzag, overlock or turn under 1 cm and press.
Fold up on the fold line, press, and pin. Sew with a blind hem stitch by hand, or by machine.
Press again from the wrong side. Check both legs are the same length by folding the trousers in half.

blocks.text: Hand blind hem or machine hem?

head: Garment
Best hem
Why
rows: Hand blind hem or machine blind hem
Stitches must be invisible from the outside
Machine topstitch with strong thread, stitch length about 3 mm, denim needle
Jeans are expected to show a stitched hem; hand stitches wear out
Strength matters; children are hard on clothes
Blind hem for straight styles, narrow machine hem of 1 to 2 cm for flared styles
A deep hem does not lie flat on a curved edge

blocks.text: Sewing on a button with a thread shank

A button sewn flat against the fabric is hard to fasten and pulls loose. The fix is a **thread shank**: a short stem of thread between the button and the fabric, about the thickness of the fabric around the buttonhole.

items: Mark the position by closing the garment and pushing a pin through the buttonhole into the fabric beneath.
Use a double thread with a knot. Bring the needle up from the wrong side at the mark.
Place a pin or matchstick across the top of the button and sew over it, passing up and down through the holes six to eight times. For a four-hole button, sew each pair of holes.
Remove the pin or matchstick and lift the button away from the fabric.
Wrap the thread three or four times tightly around the stitches under the button to form the shank.
Pass the needle to the wrong side and finish with two locking stitches.

blocks.text: Some buttons already have a **shank**: a small loop or stem on the back, common on coats and blazers. Sew these with four to six passes through the loop, keeping the loop in line with the buttonhole so the button does not twist. On a coat or any garment where the button takes strain, sew a small flat button on the inside directly behind it at the same time. This **stay button** spreads the pull so the fabric does not tear. Metal jeans buttons are not sewn at all; they are fixed with a hammer-on tack, and replacement sets are sold in markets.

blocks.title: Button with a thread shank
items: Mark through buttonhole
Double thread, knot
Sew over a pin
Wrap to form shank
Lock on wrong side
blocks.caption: The pin creates space for the shank so the button fastens easily.

blocks.title: Worked example: costing a hemming job
blocks.context: For example, Kemi runs a home repair service in Ibadan. A customer brings two pairs of office trousers to hem by hand. Prices below are approximate and only for illustration; check your own market.
steps: Thread: one reel costs about ₦500 (approximate) and does many jobs. She estimates thread for two hems at about ₦50.
Time: about 40 minutes per pair, so 80 minutes for both.
She values her time at about ₦1,500 per hour (approximate), so 80 minutes is about ₦2,000.
Light and other running costs: she adds about ₦200 for the job.
Total cost = ₦50 + ₦2,000 + ₦200 = ₦2,250. She checks what nearby tailors charge for a hand hem and sets ₦1,500 per pair (approximate), ₦3,000 for both.
blocks.result: Kemi charges ₦3,000 (approximate) for the two pairs, which covers her costs, including pay for her time, with about ₦750 left as profit, and stays in line with local prices.

blocks.title: Keep spare buttons
blocks.text: Buy a few cards of common shirt buttons in white, black and navy. Many customers lose the original, and having a close match ready lets you finish the job the same day.

takeaways: Measure both legs separately and mark the fold line and cutting line before cutting
Use invisible blind hems on formal trousers and topstitched hems on jeans
A thread shank lets a button fasten easily and stops it pulling loose
Cost every job from materials, time and running costs, then compare local prices

activity.title: Hem and button practice
steps: Shorten an old pair of trousers by 3 cm using the method above, with a blind hem on one leg and a machine hem on the other.
Compare both legs: same length, invisible on the outside, flat after pressing?
Sew one two-hole and one four-hole button onto a scrap with a thread shank.
Write a costing for the hem using your own local prices.
activity.evidence: Before and after photos of the trouser hem (outside and inside), a photo of the buttons, and your costing note.

lessons.title: Replacing zips and mending seams, tears and holes
objectives: Decide whether a faulty zip needs a new slider or full replacement
Replace a centred skirt zip using a zipper foot
Mend a split machine seam so it holds
Patch a tear and darn a small hole

blocks.text: A broken zip can make a good skirt, bag or trouser useless, so customers will pay for a quick, neat replacement. Seam splits, tears and small holes are just as common. In this lesson you learn to judge the damage first, then fix it in the way that will last.

blocks.name: black-scissors
blocks.caption: Unpicking carefully is half of every zip replacement.

blocks.text: First, diagnose the zip

items: **Teeth are fine but the zip splits open behind the slider:** the slider is often worn and has spread. Sometimes a new slider of the same size fixes it without removing the zip.
**Teeth are missing or broken, or the tape is torn:** replace the whole zip.
**Pull tab has snapped off:** a replacement pull or a small split ring can be fitted.
**Zip is stiff:** rub a little candle wax or dry soap along the teeth before deciding it is faulty.

blocks.text: Replacing a centred skirt zip

A **centred zip** sits behind a seam with stitching an equal distance on each side of the teeth. It is common on the back seam of skirts and gowns. You need a new zip of the same length (or a little longer), a **zipper foot**, which lets the needle sew close to the teeth, and matching thread.

items: Before unpicking, photograph the old zip and note where the stitching sits and how the top is finished at the waistband or facing.
Unpick the old zip with a seam ripper. Remove all loose thread ends.
Press the seam allowances back along the original fold lines.
Pin the new zip face down behind the opening, with the teeth exactly centred on the seam line and the top stop just below the waist seam allowance.
Hand baste (tack) with running stitch about 6 mm from the teeth on each side, then remove the pins. Basting stops the zip from shifting.
With the zipper foot, machine stitch down one side, across the bottom just below the bottom stop, and up the other side. Move the slider out of the way as you go.
Remove the basting, close the waistband or facing, and press from the wrong side with a cloth.

blocks.title: Never sew over metal teeth
blocks.text: Sewing across metal teeth or the stops breaks the needle and can throw pieces towards your eyes. Turn the hand wheel slowly by hand near the bottom stop, and keep your face back from the needle.
Mending a split machine seam

Turn the garment inside out. Find where the stitching has broken. Begin machine stitching 1 to 2 cm before the break, on top of the old stitching line, and continue 1 to 2 cm beyond it. Lock both ends. If the seam allowance has frayed away, sew a fraction inside the old line and finish the raw edge with zigzag.
Patching and darning

For a **tear** (a straight or L-shaped rip), place a patch of similar fabric behind it on the wrong side, larger than the tear by about 2 cm on every side, with the grain matching. Turn the patch edges under or zigzag them. Bring the torn edges together on the right side and stitch over them with a small zigzag or many short rows of straight stitching. For a **small hole** in a knit or sock, **darning** weaves new thread across the hole: first a row of parallel stitches in one direction, then weave over and under them at right angles.

blocks.title: Choosing the right fix
items: Is the damage on a seam?
Yes: restitch seam line
No: tear or hole?
Tear: patch behind
Small hole: darn
blocks.caption: Look at where the damage is before choosing a method.

blocks.title: Worked example: zip or slider?
blocks.context: For example, Chioma brings Uche a jeans skirt. The zip teeth are all present, but the zip opens behind the slider when she sits down.
steps: Uche checks the teeth: none missing, tape not torn.
She sees the slider gaps slightly at the back, a sign of wear.
She explains the two options: replace the slider, or replace the whole zip if a matching slider cannot be found.

She finds a slider of the same size number (often stamped on the back of the old slider) at the market, removes the top stops with pliers, slides the new slider on from the top, and fits new top stops.
She tests the zip ten times and tells Chioma it is working.
blocks.result: The repair takes about 20 minutes and costs much less than a full zip replacement. If the slider had not matched, Uche would have replaced the zip.

blocks.title: Buy the right zip
blocks.text: Common zips are nylon coil (light garments), plastic moulded and metal (jeans, bags). Jackets need a separating (open-ended) zip. Take the old zip to the market to match type and length.

takeaways: Diagnose first: a worn slider can sometimes be replaced without a new zip
Baste a new zip in place, then sew with a zipper foot about 6 mm from the teeth
Restitch split seams over the old line, overlapping 1 to 2 cm at each end
Patch tears from behind with matched grain; darn small holes in knits

activity.title: Zip and mend practice
steps: Take an old skirt, bag or trouser with a zip and photograph the zip before you begin.
Unpick and replace the zip using the centred method (or practise on two scraps sewn together).
Mend one split seam and one tear or hole on an old garment.
Photograph each repair from the outside and the inside.
activity.evidence: Before and after photos of the zip and the two repairs, inside and outside.

quiz.q: Ngozi's stitches have a tangle of loops on the underside. What should she try first?
options: Rethread the upper thread with the presser foot up
quiz.explain: Loops underneath usually mean the upper thread missed the tension discs or take-up lever. Rethread with the foot raised.

quiz.q: Which needle size suits denim jeans best?
quiz.explain: Heavy denim needs a strong needle such as 100/16. Fine sizes bend or break on thick fabric.

quiz.q: Why place a pin or matchstick on top of a button while sewing it on?
options: To keep the button straight for photos
To create space for a thread shank
quiz.explain: The pin holds the button away from the fabric, leaving thread for a shank so the button fastens easily.

quiz.q: A zip opens behind the slider but no teeth are missing. What is a sensible first option?
options: Replace the slider with one of the same size
quiz.explain: A worn slider that has spread is a common cause. A matching new slider can fix it without replacing the whole zip.

quiz.q: When restitching a split seam by machine, where should you start?
options: Exactly at the start of the split
1 to 2 cm before the split, on the old stitching line
In the middle of the split
2 cm inside the seam allowance edge
quiz.explain: Overlapping into sound stitching by 1 to 2 cm at both ends stops the seam splitting again at the same place.

quiz.q: Kemi's costs for a hemming job are thread ₦50, time ₦2,000 and running costs ₦200 (approximate). What is her total cost?
quiz.explain: ₦50 + ₦2,000 + ₦200 = ₦2,250. Her price must be above this to make a profit.

modules.title: Fit Alterations, Quality Checks and Caring for Customers
modules.overview: This module takes you from repairs to alterations that change how a garment fits. You will take in and let out side seams with correct measurements, check every job against a clear quality standard, fix common sewing faults, and run each order with a job card, honest communication and respect for the customer's privacy.

lessons.title: Taking in and letting out side seams
objectives: Calculate how far to move each seam to reduce or increase a measurement
Pin, mark and taper a new seam line smoothly into the old one
Decide whether a garment has enough seam allowance to let out
Finish and press an altered seam so it looks original

blocks.text: Many people own clothes that fit almost right: a gown that is loose at the waist after weight loss, a shirt that is boxy, a skirt that has become tight. Taking in and letting out side seams are the most requested fit alterations. The skill is in the numbers and in a smooth line, so the altered garment looks as if it was made that way.

blocks.name: dress
blocks.caption: A side-seam alteration changes the fit of a dress without changing its style.

blocks.text: The key calculation: every seam counts twice

When you move a stitching line 1 cm inward, you remove 1 cm from the front piece and 1 cm from the back piece at that seam. So the garment becomes **2 cm smaller per seam**. A garment with two side seams becomes 4 cm smaller in total. The rule is: **amount to move each seam = total reduction needed divided by (2 × number of seams you alter)**.

head: Total reduction wanted
Seams altered
Move each seam inward by
rows: 2 side seams plus centre back (3 seams)

blocks.text: Always alter both side seams by the same amount so the garment stays balanced and the side seams stay at the sides of the body. If more than about 5 cm must come out of each seam, the shape of armholes, pockets or darts may be affected; that is a bigger job and should be priced and discussed as such.
Taking in a side seam: step by step

items: Have the customer try the garment on, right side out. Pin out the extra fabric evenly at both side seams until it fits comfortably. Let her sit and raise her arms to check it is not too tight.
Measure how much you pinned at the waist, bust and hip. Write the numbers on a job card.
Remove the garment, turn it inside out and mark the new stitching line with chalk, using your measurements from the old seam line.
Taper the new line smoothly back into the old seam over about 8 to 10 cm at the top and bottom of the alteration. A sudden angle makes a visible dent.
Baste (tack) along the new line and do a second fitting. Adjust if needed.
Machine stitch the new line at about 2.5 mm, locking both ends, then remove the old stitches only where they would show on the outside.
If the seam allowance is now very wide, trim it to about 1.5 cm, or leave it if the customer may want it let out later. Finish raw edges and press.

blocks.text: Letting out: check the allowance first

You can only let out as much as the seam allowance allows. Unpick a small section of the side seam on the inside and measure. If the allowance is 2 cm, you can usually let out up to about 1 cm per seam and still keep 1 cm to hold the seam; across two side seams that gives up to 4 cm more room. On dark or shiny fabrics the old stitch holes and fold line may still show. Press with a damp pressing cloth and test on the inside first. Tell the customer honestly before you start if marks may remain.

blocks.title: Side-seam alteration workflow
items: Pin on the body
Measure and record
Mark and taper line
Baste and refit
Stitch, finish, press
blocks.caption: Every fit alteration follows this order, with a second fitting before final stitching.

blocks.title: Worked example: taking in an ankara gown
blocks.context: For example, Ruth brings Adaeze an ankara gown that is 6 cm too big at the waist and 4 cm too big at the hip. The bust fits.
steps: Adaeze divides by four for two side seams: waist 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 cm per seam; hip 4 ÷ 4 = 1 cm per seam; bust 0 cm.
She marks the new line 1.5 cm inside the old seam at the waist and 1 cm inside at the hip, on both sides.
She tapers the line back to 0 cm about 10 cm above the waist, so the bust is untouched.
She bastes, does a second fitting with Ruth, and finds the fit is right.
She stitches, finishes the edges with zigzag and presses.
blocks.result: The gown is 6 cm smaller at the waist and 4 cm smaller at the hip, with a smooth line and unchanged bust. Adaeze records the numbers on the job card in case Ruth wants it let out again.

blocks.title: Do not cut too soon
blocks.text: Leave extra seam allowance inside the garment until the customer has tried on the finished alteration. You cannot add fabric back once it is cut away.

takeaways: Moving a seam 1 cm in makes the garment 2 cm smaller at that seam
For two side seams, divide the total reduction by four
Taper new lines into old seams over about 8 to 10 cm
Check seam allowance before promising to let a garment out

activity.title: Take in a garment
steps: Choose an old shirt or dress that is loose on you or a family member.
Pin out the extra at both side seams on the body and measure the total at waist and hip.
Calculate how far to move each seam and write the numbers down.
Mark, taper, baste, refit, then stitch and press.
Measure the finished waist and hip and compare with your target.
activity.evidence: Before and after photos on the body (with permission), your calculation note and the final measurements.

lessons.title: Quality standards and fixing common sewing faults
objectives: Inspect a finished job against a clear quality checklist
Identify and correct puckering, skipped stitches and wavy seams
Press seams correctly as you sew
Decide when a job must be redone before handover

blocks.text: Customers judge a tailor by small details: a loose thread, a hem that is longer on one leg, a seam that wrinkles. These are all preventable. A written quality standard, checked on every job before handover, protects your name and brings customers back.

blocks.name: white-heavy-check-mark
blocks.caption: Check every job against the same standard before you hand it back.

blocks.text: Your handover quality checklist

items: **Stitches**: even length (about 2.5 mm for normal seams), balanced on both sides, no loops, no skipped stitches.
**Seams**: straight, at the agreed allowance, locked at both ends, no puckering.
**Symmetry**: both legs, sleeves or sides match within about 0.5 cm.
**Edges**: raw edges finished with zigzag, overlock, overcast or a turned edge, so nothing will fray.
**Fastenings**: buttons, hooks and zips open and close smoothly ten times.
**Finish**: all loose threads trimmed, chalk marks removed, garment pressed and folded or hung.

blocks.text: Common faults and how to fix them

head: Fault
Likely cause
Fix
rows: Upper tension too tight, stitch too long on fine fabric, blunt needle, pulling the fabric
Check threading, try a slightly shorter stitch on fine fabric, new fine needle, let the feed dogs move the fabric
Blunt or bent needle, wrong needle type for knits, needle inserted wrongly
Change the needle; use ballpoint for knits; check the flat side faces the right way
Do not pull; use a narrow zigzag; lighter presser foot pressure if your machine allows
Not measured on both legs; fabric shifted while sewing
Measure each leg, pin more closely, press before stitching
Catch only one or two threads of the outer fabric
Repair did not overlap old stitching; ends not locked
Overlap 1 to 2 cm each side and lock ends

blocks.text: Finishing raw edges: your options

items: **Zigzag**: sew a medium zigzag along the raw edge so the right swing of the needle falls just off the edge. Works on most domestic electric machines.

**Overlock (serger)**: a separate machine that trims and wraps the edge with three or four threads in one pass. It is what factory garments use; many tailors pay a neighbour with an overlocker a small fee per garment until they buy one.
**Hand overcast**: slow but needs no machine, ideal for a manual straight-stitch machine user.
**Turned and stitched**: fold the raw edge under about 5 mm and straight stitch it. Neat on light cotton.
**French seam**: sew wrong sides together, trim, then sew again right sides together, enclosing the raw edge. Good for sheer fabric and lace linings.
**Pinking shears**: zigzag-bladed scissors that slow fraying on firm cotton; not enough on loose weaves.

blocks.text: Match the finish to what the garment already has. If the factory edge is overlocked and you have no overlocker, a neat zigzag is an acceptable substitute; tell the customer if the finish will look different inside.
Pressing: the step beginners skip

**Pressing** is not the same as ironing. Ironing slides the iron back and forth; pressing means lifting the iron and setting it down on one area at a time, so the fabric does not stretch. Press each seam flat as sewn first, to set the stitches, then press it open or to one side. Use the right heat for the fibre, and a damp cotton pressing cloth on dark, shiny or delicate fabric to stop shine and scorching. A well-pressed alteration looks professional even when the stitching is simple.

blocks.title: The quality loop
items: Sew a section
Inspect it
Fix any fault
Press it
Move to next
blocks.caption: Checking and pressing as you go is faster than unpicking at the end.

blocks.title: Worked example: inspecting before handover
blocks.context: For example, Grace has finished hemming four pairs of school trousers for a customer and checks them against her list before the parent arrives.
steps: She folds each pair in half and checks leg lengths: three pairs match, one pair has one leg 1 cm longer.
She checks the stitching: all locked and balanced, but two pairs have loose thread ends.
She unpicks and re-hems the uneven leg, then measures again: now equal.
She trims all threads, presses each pair and folds them with a small note of the job number.
blocks.result: All four pairs pass the checklist. Ten minutes of checking saved her from a complaint and a return visit.

blocks.text: Keep a simple count of how many jobs pass first time and how many need redoing. If more than one job in ten needs a redo, look for the pattern: is it always hems, always knits, always rushed evening work? That tells you what to practise next.

blocks.title: When to redo
blocks.text: If a fault would be visible to the customer or would fail in normal wear, redo it before handover. Small honest fixes cost less than lost customers.

takeaways: Use one written checklist on every job before handover
Most stitch faults come from the needle or threading, not the tension dial
Press, do not iron, and press each seam as you sew
Track how many jobs need redoing to find what to practise

activity.title: Quality audit of your own work
steps: Write the six-point checklist on a card or in your notebook.
Inspect three pieces you made earlier in this course against it.
Record each fault you find and its cause, using the fault table.
Fix at least one fault and press the piece properly.
activity.evidence: Your completed checklist for three pieces and a before and after photo of one fault you fixed.

lessons.title: Job cards, honest service and customer privacy
objectives: Record every order on a job card with measurements, price and dates
Note existing damage and agree the work before you start
Protect customers' measurements, photos and fittings with respect
Use simple weekly numbers to track your service

blocks.text: Most quarrels between tailors and customers come from three things: unclear instructions, missed collection dates and disagreement about the price. A simple job card and a few honest habits prevent almost all of them. They also give you the records you need to see whether your business is growing.

blocks.name: clipboard
blocks.caption: A job card for every order prevents most disputes.

blocks.text: What goes on a job card

head: Field
Example entry
rows: Take in waist 6 cm, hip 4 cm; shorten hem 3 cm
Waist 78 cm, hip 102 cm, finished length 120 cm
Small stain on front, fading at hem (customer informed)
Price agreed, deposit paid, balance due on collection

blocks.text: Use a paper book with carbon copies or a page in your notebook, and give the customer the job number. Many tailors also send the details by WhatsApp so both sides have a written record. Take a photo of the garment before you start, with the customer's permission, so the condition is clear.

Keep old job cards. When a regular customer returns, her measurements and past alterations are already written down, which saves a fitting and shows her you take her business seriously. If a customer disputes what was agreed, the card written at drop-off, with her phone number and the WhatsApp copy, settles it quickly and fairly.
Honest service

items: Say plainly if a repair will not last: for example, a worn-out collar or rotten fabric around a tear.
Agree the price before starting. If you find more work once you open a seam, call the customer before doing it.
Never cut a customer's fabric without confirming the measurement with them.
Return useful offcuts and spare buttons with the garment.
Give a realistic collection date and send a message early if you will be late.

blocks.text: Privacy and respect

Body measurements and fitting photos are personal. Keep job cards where visitors cannot read them, and do not share measurements with anyone else. Ask before photographing a customer, and ask again before posting any photo online; post garments without faces unless the customer clearly agrees. Offer a private space for fittings, and let a customer bring a friend or relative. Measure children only with a parent or guardian present.

blocks.title: Fake payment alerts
blocks.text: Some people show a fake transfer screenshot or send a fake SMS alert. Before releasing a garment, confirm the money has arrived in your own bank or wallet app (for example Opay, Moniepoint or your bank app), not from the customer's phone screen.
Deposits and collection

For alterations and anything that needs materials, many tailors ask for a deposit, often part of the price, before starting. It covers your materials if a customer never returns. Write the deposit and the balance on the job card and in the WhatsApp message. Agree what happens to garments left uncollected for a long time, and write it on the card, so there is no argument months later.
Handling a complaint calmly

items: Listen fully and look at the garment together. Do not argue while the customer is still explaining.
Check the job card: was the work done as agreed and recorded?
If the fault is yours, apologise and offer to fix it free, with a clear new date.
If the request is new work, explain kindly and offer a price for the change.
Write what was agreed on the job card and keep a note of what caused the problem.

blocks.title: Life of one job
items: Receive and inspect
Record on job card
Agree price and date
Work and check
Collect and pay
blocks.caption: Every order follows the same five stages, with a written record at the start.

blocks.text: Numbers that show how you are doing

blocks.title: Worked example: a simple weekly report
blocks.context: For example, Esther takes repair and alteration jobs from home in Jos and fills in a short summary every Saturday from her job cards.
steps: Jobs received this week: 14. Jobs collected: 12.
Jobs finished by the promised date: 11 of 12, so 92% on time.
Jobs that needed a redo before handover: 1 of 12.
Money received: she adds up the paid balances and deposits from her job cards and checks them against her bank app.
Most common job: hems (6), then zips (3).
blocks.result: Esther sees that hems are her main work, that she is almost always on time, and that she should buy more hem thread and practise zips to speed them up.

blocks.text: Write your weekly numbers in the same notebook every week. After a month you will see trends: which jobs bring the most money, which days are busiest and whether late jobs are rising.

takeaways: Give every order a job card with measurements, condition, price and date
Agree changes before doing extra work, and never cut without confirming
Keep measurements private and ask before taking or posting photos
Confirm payment in your own app before releasing a garment

activity.title: Set up your job card system
steps: Draw a job card template in your notebook with the eight fields above.
Fill in job cards for at least two real or practice jobs, including condition notes.
Send one customer (or a family member acting as one) the job details by WhatsApp.
At the end of the week, write a five-line summary like Esther's.
activity.evidence: Photos of two completed job cards (hide phone numbers) and your weekly summary.

quiz.q: Adaeze must make a gown 8 cm smaller at the waist using only the two side seams. How far should she move each seam?
quiz.explain: Each seam removes double its movement, and there are two seams: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 cm per seam.

quiz.q: Why taper a new side seam back into the old seam over 8 to 10 cm?
options: To avoid a visible dent or angle in the seam
quiz.explain: A sudden change in seam line shows as a dent. A gradual taper keeps the line smooth.

quiz.q: A customer wants a skirt let out by 6 cm. The side seam allowance is 1.5 cm. What should you do?
options: Cut new seam allowance from the hem
Stretch the fabric with a hot iron
Explain that only about 1 to 2 cm in total is possible and discuss options
quiz.explain: With 1.5 cm allowance, you can let out about 0.5 cm per seam and still keep 1 cm, about 2 cm in total. Be honest before starting.

quiz.q: A knit T-shirt seam comes out wavy. What is the most likely cause?
quiz.explain: Pulling knit fabric through the machine stretches it, and the seam stays wavy. Let the feed dogs move it.

quiz.q: A customer shows a transfer screenshot and wants to collect her gown. What should you do?
options: Release it, the screenshot is proof
Confirm the money is in your own bank or wallet app first
Ask her to send the screenshot again
quiz.explain: Screenshots and SMS alerts can be faked. Check your own account balance before releasing the garment.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between pressing and ironing?
options: Pressing lifts and sets the iron down without sliding
quiz.explain: Pressing sets the iron down on one area at a time, so the fabric and seams do not stretch out of shape.

modules.title: Pricing, Portfolio and Growing a Home Tailoring Service
modules.overview: Good work becomes income when it is priced correctly, shown clearly and offered to the right people. In this module you build a price list from real costs, create a before-and-after portfolio and WhatsApp Business catalogue, and complete your capstone with a 90-day plan for your service.

lessons.title: Costing every job and building a price list
objectives: Separate materials, labour and running costs for a job
Spread monthly running costs fairly across jobs
Set a price with a profit margin and compare it with local prices
Build a simple price list for your main services

blocks.text: Many beginner tailors set prices by guessing or by copying the cheapest person on the street, then wonder why they work hard and have nothing left. A price must cover four things: the **materials** used, your **time** (labour), your **running costs** (overheads) and a **profit** that lets you save, replace tools and grow.

blocks.name: abacus
blocks.caption: Every price is built from materials, time, running costs and profit.

blocks.text: The four parts of a price

items: **Materials**: zip, thread, buttons, interfacing, patch fabric. Count only what the job uses; a reel of thread does many jobs.
**Labour**: minutes spent × the value of your time per hour. Decide a fair hourly value and use it consistently.
**Running costs**: generator fuel or electricity, needles, machine oil and servicing, data for WhatsApp, transport to the market. Add them up for a month and share them across your jobs.
**Profit**: an extra percentage on top of costs, often 20 to 30% for small service work. Profit is not the same as your pay; your pay is already in labour.

blocks.text: Sharing monthly running costs

Add up your running costs for a typical month and divide by the number of jobs you usually do. For example, if running costs are about ₦12,000 (approximate) a month and you do about 60 jobs, each job carries about ₦200 of running costs. Recalculate every few months, because fuel and data prices change.

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing a zip replacement
blocks.context: For example, Funke repairs clothes from home in Abeokuta. All prices are approximate and for illustration only; use your own market prices.
steps: Materials: zip ₦500 + thread about ₦50 = ₦550.
Labour: about 45 minutes. At ₦1,500 per hour, 45 minutes = 0.75 × ₦1,500 = ₦1,125.
Running costs share: about ₦200 per job.
She checks local prices: nearby tailors charge between ₦2,000 and ₦3,000 (approximate). She rounds to ₦2,500.
blocks.result: Funke's price of ₦2,500 (approximate) covers her materials, pays her time, carries its share of running costs and leaves a profit. She knows she is not working at a loss.

blocks.title: What a price is built from
items: Profit
Running costs share
Labour (your time)
Materials
blocks.caption: Materials and time form the base; running costs and profit sit on top and must never be left out.

blocks.text: Building your price list

head: Service
Typical time (beginner)
Price range to check locally
rows: Small charge, often grouped per garment

blocks.text: Time each job for your first few weeks and write it down. You will get faster, which lets you either lower your prices to win customers or keep them and earn more per hour. Express prices as **from** a figure (for example, "zip replacement from ₦2,500") so you can charge more for difficult fabrics, linings or rush work.
Rush jobs, bulk jobs and discounts

Charge extra for same-day work, because it pushes other jobs back. Offer a small discount for bulk work, such as hemming ten school trousers for one family or uniforms for a small school, because one fitting and one handover serve many items. Never discount below your total cost.
Pricing simple made items

For a made item such as a pillowcase or tote bag, measure the fabric it uses in cm and work out its share of the fabric price. For example, if a length of fabric 110 cm wide and 100 cm long costs about ₦3,000 (approximate) and a tote bag uses a piece 110 cm × 45 cm, the bag uses 45% of it, about ₦1,350, before thread, lining or straps. Then add labour, running costs and profit exactly as for repairs.
Getting paid smoothly

Decide your payment rules and say them up front: deposit at drop-off for alterations and materials, balance at collection. Accept cash and transfers. Give your account name clearly and check every transfer in your own app before handing over the garment. Write each payment on the job card the same day, so your weekly numbers are correct.

blocks.title: Write prices where customers see them
blocks.text: Post your price list as a WhatsApp status and pin it in your catalogue. Clear prices reduce haggling and help customers trust you.

blocks.title: Do not undercut yourself
blocks.text: If you price below cost to beat a neighbour, you lose money on every job. Compete on quality, speed and reliability instead.

takeaways: Price = materials + labour + running costs share + profit
Share monthly running costs across your usual number of jobs
Time your jobs, then compare your price with local tailors
Charge more for rush work and never discount below cost

activity.title: Make your price list
steps: List your monthly running costs and divide by your expected number of jobs.
Cost three services (for example a hem, a zip and a take-in) using the four parts.
Ask three local tailors or check WhatsApp statuses for their prices.
Set your price for each service and write a price list.
activity.evidence: Your costing sheet for three services and a photo or screenshot of your price list.

lessons.title: Before-and-after portfolio and finding customers
objectives: Take clear before-and-after photos of repairs and alterations
Set up a WhatsApp Business profile and catalogue
Describe your service clearly to customers and partners
Find steady sources of repair work in your community

blocks.text: People trust what they can see. A clear before-and-after photo of a neat zip, an invisible hem or a gown that now fits does more selling than any message. In this lesson you build a small portfolio, put it on WhatsApp Business and look for places where repair work comes in regularly. Start with the pieces you made in this course; you do not need paying customers to begin.

blocks.name: product-photography
blocks.caption: Good before-and-after photos are your strongest advertisement.

blocks.text: Taking good before-and-after photos

items: Shoot in daylight near a window or outdoors in shade. Avoid harsh direct sun and flash, which flatten colour.
Lay the garment flat on a plain sheet or hang it on a hanger against a plain wall.
Take the before photo from the same angle and distance you will use for the after photo.
Take a close-up of the repair itself: the zip, the hem stitching, the patched area.
For alterations, take on-body photos only with the customer's permission, and crop out the face unless she agrees.
Name the files or label them in your gallery with the job number.

blocks.text: Setting up WhatsApp Business

WhatsApp Business is a free app from WhatsApp for small businesses. It lets you create a business profile with your name, address area, hours and a short description, add a **catalogue** of services with photos and prices, set a greeting message and quick replies, and label chats (for example "new order", "ready for collection"). Use a separate number from your personal one if you can, so work messages stay organised.

items: **Profile description**: one clear line, for example "Clothing repairs and alterations: hems, zips, buttons, fit. Pick-up in Ikeja."
**Catalogue items**: one item per service, each with a before-and-after photo and a "from" price.
**Status**: post one finished job a day or a few times a week, with the customer's permission.
**Quick replies**: save your price list and collection rules so you can answer fast.

blocks.title: Weak message versus strong message
items: Weak
Strong
blocks.caption: A specific message with proof and a clear next step gets replies.

blocks.text: Answering enquiries well

items: Reply within a few hours during working hours. Use a quick reply for your greeting and price list.
Ask for a photo of the garment and the problem, so you can quote accurately.
Give a price range and a collection date, and say what could change the price (for example lining or a heavy fabric).
Confirm drop-off or pick-up time and send the job number once you receive the item.
Message the customer when the job is ready, with a photo of the finished work.

blocks.text: Many customers have costly data. Keep photos clear but not huge, and send one or two good pictures rather than ten. Short voice notes are fine for explaining options, but always confirm the price and date in writing so both of you can refer back to it.
Where steady work comes from

items: **Schools and uniforms**: parents need hems and repairs at the start of every term.
**Dry cleaners and laundries**: they often see damaged clothes and can refer customers or send you repairs.
**Fabric and ready-made clothing sellers**: customers buying ready-made clothes often need hems or fitting.
**Churches, mosques and community groups**: events and festive seasons bring alteration rushes.
**Offices and estates**: offer a weekly pick-up day for busy workers.

blocks.title: Worked example: a partner referral
blocks.context: For example, Patience lives near a busy dry cleaner in Port Harcourt. She has twelve before-and-after photos and a printed price list.
steps: She visits the dry cleaner, shows her photos and explains her services and turnaround time.
She offers to collect repair items twice a week and return them finished, so the cleaner can offer repairs to its customers.
They agree that the cleaner adds a small amount on top of her price when charging its customers.
She keeps a job card for each item and returns work on the agreed days.
blocks.result: Patience gains a steady flow of repair jobs without advertising, and the dry cleaner gains a new service. Clear records keep the partnership smooth.

blocks.title: Pick-ups and deliveries
blocks.text: When collecting or delivering clothes, meet in daylight at a public or familiar place where possible, tell someone at home where you are going, and do not share your home address publicly on your status. Give the full address only to confirmed customers.

blocks.title: Ask for reviews
blocks.text: After a happy collection, ask the customer to send a short message you can share (with her permission), or simply to tell friends. Word of mouth is still how most home tailors grow.

takeaways: Shoot before and after from the same angle, in daylight, on a plain background
WhatsApp Business gives you a profile, catalogue, quick replies and labels
A strong message names the service, shows proof, gives a price and a next step
Schools, dry cleaners, clothing sellers and community groups bring steady work

Install WhatsApp Business and complete the profile description, hours and area.
Add at least three services to the catalogue, each with a photo and a "from" price.
Write and post one status advert using the strong message format.
List three possible partners near you (school, cleaner, clothing seller) and visit one.

lessons.title: Your capstone portfolio and 90-day plan
objectives: Complete five repair or alteration jobs and one simple made item to the course standard
Assemble an evidence pack with job cards, photos, costings and feedback
Reflect honestly on what changed after feedback
Write a 90-day plan with weekly targets

blocks.text: Your capstone proves you can do the work, not just describe it. You will complete a set of real jobs, check them against your quality standard, cost them and collect feedback. Then you will plan the next 90 days of your service. Take your time: an honest, complete pack is worth more than a rushed one.

blocks.name: portfolio
blocks.caption: Your capstone pack shows real jobs, real numbers and real feedback.

blocks.text: The capstone jobs

items: **Button**: sew on at least two buttons with thread shanks.
**Hem**: shorten one pair of trousers or a skirt with an invisible hem.
**Zip**: replace or repair one zip.
**Seam or tear repair**: mend one split seam, patch or darn.
**Fit alteration**: take in or let out one garment at the side seams.
**Simple made item**: sew one pillowcase, apron or tote bag from new fabric, with finished seams and edges.

blocks.text: Use real customers or family members where you can. Each job needs a job card, before-and-after photos, a quality checklist and a costing. For the made item, cut on the straight grain, use a 1 to 1.5 cm seam allowance, finish all raw edges and press.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning a pillowcase
blocks.context: For example, Mary chooses an envelope pillowcase for a pillow about 50 cm × 75 cm as her made item.
steps: Width: pillow width 50 cm + 2 seam allowances of 1.5 cm = 53 cm.
Length: front 75 cm + back 75 cm + 18 cm envelope overlap + 2 hems using 2.5 cm each = 173 cm. She cuts one strip 53 cm × 173 cm on the straight grain.
She hems both short ends, turning under 1 cm and then 1.5 cm, so each hem uses 2.5 cm and the strip is now 168 cm long.
She folds the strip, right sides together, so the hemmed ends overlap by 18 cm and the folded piece measures 75 cm, then stitches both sides at 1.5 cm.
She zigzags the raw edges, turns it right side out, and presses.
blocks.result: The pillowcase fits a 50 cm × 75 cm pillow with an overlap that keeps it closed without buttons. Mary records fabric used, time and cost.

blocks.text: Your evidence pack

blocks.title: Capstone evidence checklist
items: Six job cards
Before-and-after photos
Quality checklists passed
Costing sheet
Two customer feedback notes
Reflection and 90-day plan
blocks.caption: Tick every item before you attempt the final quiz.

blocks.text: Reflection: what changed after feedback

Write half a page. What did customers or family say about your work? Which job was hardest, and why? What did you change, for example measuring both legs, using a new needle, or pressing more carefully, and did the next job improve? Honest reflection is part of the assessment; nobody expects a beginner to be perfect. Include one photo of an early piece next to a later one so the improvement is visible.
Your 90-day plan

head: Period
Focus
Example targets
rows: 10 paid jobs, all on job cards, no more than 1 redo
WhatsApp catalogue complete, 1 partner (cleaner, school or seller), 20 paid jobs
Hem time cut by a third, learn one new skill (for example lined zips or sleeve shortening), decide on next equipment

blocks.text: Equipment decisions should follow demand. If you are paying for overlocking on most jobs, an overlocker may be your next purchase. If you sew for many hours a day, an industrial straight-stitch machine is faster and more durable than a domestic one. Save part of each job's profit towards the tool you need most. When your service is steady, you may also consider registering a business name with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC), which can help with bank accounts and larger customers.
Submitting your capstone

items: Put all photos for each job in one album or folder named with the job number.
Scan or photograph your job cards, checklists and costing sheet clearly.
Type or photograph your reflection and 90-day plan.
Check every item on the evidence checklist, then upload your pack in the WODDI Institute app.
Confirm in the app that the practical task is complete, then take the final quiz.

blocks.text: To earn the certificate you must complete the practical capstone and score at least 70% in the final quiz. If you score lower, review the modules where you missed questions and try again. Keep your evidence pack after submission; it doubles as your first business portfolio.

blocks.title: Keep learning from others
blocks.text: Many skilled tailors learned by working beside an experienced tailor. Spending time in a busy shop, even part-time, teaches speed, finishing and customer handling that no course can fully replace.

takeaways: The capstone covers buttons, a hem, a zip, a repair, a fit alteration and one made item
Every job needs a job card, photos, a quality check and a costing
Honest reflection on feedback is part of the assessment
Plan 90 days in three stages and let demand guide equipment purchases

steps: Complete the six capstone jobs, each with a job card and before-and-after photos.

quiz.q: Funke's costs for a job are materials ₦550, labour ₦1,125 and running costs ₦200 (approximate). With a 20% profit, what is the price before rounding?
quiz.explain: Total cost is ₦1,875. 20% of that is ₦375, so the price is ₦2,250 before rounding.

quiz.q: Monthly running costs are about ₦12,000 and you do about 60 jobs. What running cost should each job carry?
Which message is most likely to bring a customer?
options: Hems, zips and fit alterations, before-and-after photo, from ₦2,500, ready in 2 days
quiz.explain: A strong message names the service, shows proof, gives a price and a clear time frame.

quiz.q: Why should before and after photos be taken from the same angle?
options: So the change is clear and believable
quiz.explain: Matching angles let viewers compare directly, which makes the improvement clear and trustworthy.

quiz.q: Mary's pillow is 50 cm wide and she uses 1.5 cm seam allowances on both sides. How wide should she cut the fabric?
Grace pays a neighbour to overlock edges on almost every job. What does this suggest for her 90-day plan?
options: An overlocker may be her next equipment purchase
quiz.explain: Equipment decisions should follow demand. Paying for overlocking on most jobs is a sign an overlocker would pay for itself.

finalQuiz.q: A customer's jersey gown has a split seam. Which fabric type is it and what stitch should you use?
finalQuiz.explain: Jersey is a knit fabric. A narrow zigzag stretches with it so the seam does not snap.

finalQuiz.q: Which hand stitch is invisible from the outside and used on trouser hems?
finalQuiz.explain: The blind hem stitch catches only one or two threads of the outer fabric, so it does not show.

finalQuiz.q: Trousers are 5 cm too long with a 3 cm hem. Keeping a 4 cm hem, how much do you trim?
finalQuiz.explain: Below the new fold there is 5 + 3 = 8 cm. Keep 4 cm and trim 4 cm.

finalQuiz.q: What should you always do before threading the upper thread of a sewing machine?
options: Raise the presser foot and bring the needle to its highest point
finalQuiz.explain: A raised presser foot opens the tension discs, and the needle and take-up lever must be at the top for correct threading.

finalQuiz.q: A machine starts skipping stitches on cotton after weeks of use. What is the most likely fix?
finalQuiz.explain: A blunt or bent needle is the most common cause of skipped stitches. Change it first.

finalQuiz.q: When sewing on a flat button, what creates the thread shank?
options: Sewing over a pin, then wrapping the thread under the button
finalQuiz.explain: The pin leaves slack; wrapping the slack under the button forms the shank.

finalQuiz.q: When replacing a skirt zip by machine, which presser foot do you use?
finalQuiz.explain: A zipper foot lets the needle sew close to the zip teeth.

finalQuiz.q: A dress must be 4 cm smaller at the waist using two side seams. How far is each seam moved in?
finalQuiz.explain: Each seam removes double its movement: 4 ÷ (2 × 2) = 1 cm per seam.

finalQuiz.q: Which item belongs on a job card to prevent disputes about existing damage?
options: Condition notes and a before photo
finalQuiz.explain: Recording stains, wear or damage at drop-off, with a photo, shows the condition before you worked on it.

finalQuiz.q: Funke's total cost for a job is ₦2,000 (approximate). She adds 25% profit. What is her price?
finalQuiz.explain: 25% of ₦2,000 is ₦500, so the price is ₦2,500.

finalQuiz.q: Which is the best way to post a fitting photo of a customer on your WhatsApp status?
options: Post it with her face, she will not mind
Ask her permission and crop out the face unless she agrees
finalQuiz.explain: Photos and measurements are personal. Ask permission and protect identity unless she clearly agrees.

finalQuiz.q: What must you complete to earn this course certificate?
options: The practical capstone and at least 70% in the final quiz
finalQuiz.explain: Certification requires both the practical capstone evidence and a final quiz score of at least 70%.
